scenes.tts: Shine steady light, at a power people routinely use, on the striatum of a mouse that carries no opsin at all. Its firing rate falls. Lit on one side, a freely moving mouse turns toward that side. Owen, Liu and Kreitzer reported both in wild-type mice. So what does a light-on, light-off comparison show? It compares light with no light, in animals that happen to carry an opsin.
scenes.visual: A cell with no opsin gets light; firing falls and the animal turns; the light-on/off comparison is relabelled light versus no light.

scenes.tts: A recording tells you that activity goes with a behaviour. It cannot tell you whether the activity produces it. So change the activity on purpose. Drive the cells, and you ask whether their activity is sufficient. Suppress them, and you ask whether it is necessary. Both answers hold only for the cells you targeted, the time you illuminated, and the assay you scored.
scenes.visual: Cells and behaviour joined by a dashed 'goes with' link; light drives or suppresses the cells; sufficient and necessary questions; three limits.

scenes.tts: The minimum design crosses construct with light. Opsin with light. Opsin without light. Fluorophore only with light. Fluorophore only without light. The quantity you care about is the interaction. That is the extra effect of light in animals that carry the opsin.
scenes.visual: A two-by-two grid fills cell by cell; a gold bracket marks the extra effect of light with the opsin.

scenes.tts: A usable claim names the cells, the projection, the timing and the behaviour. Tye and colleagues lit basolateral amygdala terminals in the central amygdala, in freely moving mice. Activating those terminals reduced anxiety-related behaviour. But light there can also excite axons passing through, and drive the parent cell bodies. So they blocked glutamate receptors locally in the central amygdala. That abolished the light-induced reduction.
scenes.visual: Boxes for the two regions; light on the terminals; two question marks for passing axons and parent cell bodies; a receptor block removes the reduction.

scenes.tts: Now the arithmetic, with numbers invented for teaching. A pilot gives sixty seconds of avoidance with the opsin, and forty-eight with the fluorophore alone, both lit. The pooled standard deviation is twelve seconds. The difference divided by that spread is an effect size of one. For eighty percent power and a two-sided alpha of zero point zero five, that needs sixteen animals per group. But if the true effect is half as big, it needs sixty-three.
scenes.visual: Two bars, the effect size worked out, and a curve of animals per group against effect size with two points.
scenes.caption: Now the arithmetic, with numbers invented for teaching. A pilot gives 60 seconds of avoidance with the opsin, and 48 with the fluorophore alone, both lit. The pooled standard deviation is 12 seconds. The difference divided by that spread is an effect size of 1. For 80% power and a two-sided alpha of 0.05, that needs 16 animals per group. But if the true effect is half as big, it needs 63.

scenes.tts: Count animals, not trials. Eight mice with forty trials each are eight animals with trials nested inside them, not three hundred twenty independent observations. And a small pilot is noisy, and the pilot that overshoots is the one followed up, so the effect carried forward tends to be too big. So power the study on the smallest effect you would care about. Control for the light, and size for the smaller effect.
